summary: Presents an object-oriented information model for representing policy information, developed with the DMTF's Common Information Model. It gives a common vocabulary for describing rules that govern network behavior. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3060 defines a shared model for describing policies as rules with conditions and actions. It standardizes the concepts and relationships, but a separate data model is needed before software can implement them.

questions: what is the policy core information model
what is a policy rule in pcim
how do policy conditions work in dnf and cnf
subtitle: A shared information model for representing network policies as rules, conditions, and actions.

tldr.problem: Policy systems need a common way to describe rules and their relationships without tying those descriptions to one repository or implementation.
tldr.mechanism: PCIM defines object classes for policy groups, rules, conditions, actions, and time periods, plus associations that describe how instances relate.
tldr.outcome: PCIM is an information model, not a protocol or directly implementable data format. It must be mapped to a concrete data model, and RFC 3460 updates it.

today: RFC 3060 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2001. The unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 3460.

sections.title: What the Policy Model Describes
sections.content:
The Policy Core Information Model (PCIM) is an object-oriented model for representing policy information. It was developed in the IETF Policy Framework work and as an extension to the DMTF Common Information Model.

PCIM defines classes for policy information and control, and association classes that express relationships between instances. It is generic rather than tied to a policy domain, repository, or access protocol; later documents can map it to implementations such as LDAP.
sections.plainLanguage: PCIM defines common concepts for describing policies. It leaves the storage format and implementation details to other specifications.

sections.title: Rules, Groups and Priorities
sections.content:
A policy rule connects conditions to actions. The conditions decide whether the rule applies; if their combined result is true, the rule's actions may run. Rules can be placed in policy groups, and groups can contain other groups, but one group contains rules or groups rather than both.

Rules can have priorities to resolve conflicts. A larger priority value wins. The model is declarative: it defines building blocks and relationships, but does not prescribe the algorithm that evaluates every policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy rule says when it applies and what actions follow. If matching rules conflict, the rule with the higher priority takes precedence.

sections.title: Classes and Their Relationships
sections.content:
PCIM has structural classes for policies and association classes for relationships. The central classes include PolicyGroup, PolicyRule, PolicyCondition, and PolicyAction. A policy repository can hold reusable policy information.

Conditions and actions can be specific to one rule or designed for reuse. This distinction reflects the administrator's intent and affects naming, access control, and how an item is managed in a repository.
sections.plainLanguage: PCIM separates the kinds of policy objects from the links between them. A condition or action can belong to one rule or be stored for reuse.

sections.title: Combining Conditions and Actions
sections.content:
A rule combines conditions using either disjunctive normal form (DNF) or conjunctive normal form (CNF). In DNF, groups of conditions joined by AND are joined by OR. In CNF, groups joined by OR are joined by AND. Individual conditions may be negated.

The ConditionListType property selects the form and defaults to DNF. The association between a rule and each condition identifies its group and whether it is negated. Actions can also have an indicated execution order, which may be mandatory, recommended, or unimportant.
sections.plainLanguage: PCIM gives a rule two standard ways to combine yes-or-no conditions. The selected form determines how condition groups produce the final result that controls the actions.

sections.title: Roles and Time Periods
sections.content:
Roles select the policies that apply to a resource. Administrators can assign multiple roles, and PCIM represents a role combination as names joined by &&; the names in a combination are in alphabetical order. A policy decision point expands combinations to retrieve relevant policies.

PolicyTimePeriodCondition represents when a rule is active. It can combine a calendar range with month, day-of-month, day-of-week, and time-of-day fields. The fields in one condition are combined with AND; times are either local time or UTC, with UTC as the default.
sections.plainLanguage: Roles help select policies for resources with particular functions or combinations of functions. Time conditions let a rule apply only during a specified schedule.

sections.title: Vendor Extensions
sections.content:
VendorPolicyCondition and VendorPolicyAction provide extension points for conditions and actions not described by the core model. Their data is an octet string, and an object identifier names its encoding and meaning.

A policy decision point can compare the identifier with the formats it recognizes. The RFC intends these classes for vendor-specific extensions, not standardized extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The model provides vendor extension classes for condition or action data it does not define. An identifier tells a reader which format the data uses.

sections.title: Security Depends on the Implementation
sections.content:
PCIM does not define a protocol, repository, access method, or concrete implementation, so it has no specific security requirements of its own. It is an information model that must be mapped to a data model before implementation.

Each real application of PCIM must define its security requirements. Derived data models must explain how they protect policy values and relationships from unauthorized reading or modification and how they authenticate administrators and users where needed.
sections.plainLanguage: PCIM describes policy information but does not implement access controls or other security mechanisms. Each concrete system built from it must define and provide the security it needs.
